text: Rover deployment provide a framework of common issues to address during the design of any future AMD implementation project. The most significant hurdles to efficient AV operations faced by the Mines Rover AV deployment were as follows: • AV shuttle’s speed differential with other conventional vehicles. This issue provides one of the most relevant challenges to any AV deployment where the design for the fleet AV’s operating speeds is lower than the typical operating speeds of other conventional, human-operated vehicles. With the vehicles operating at 12 mph in mixed traffic, conflicts between the AV shuttles with conventional human-operated vehicles occasionally occurred. In these interactions, human drivers typically became impatient with the AV shuttle and at times began following too closely behind the shuttle while seeking an opportunity to overtake the shuttle. In addition, human drivers would merge abruptly in front of the shuttles (i.e., cut them off) and unknowingly trigger emergency stops. A significant crash occurred when a shuttle was rear-ended by a driver not properly judging the slow operating speed of the AV. • Impacts of terrain. The impact of operating the vehicle on the deployment site’s terrain generated major maintenance costs and impacted operational reliability. The Colorado School of Mines campus is located in Golden, Colorado, in the foothills of the Rocky Mountains. The steep hills that the AV shuttles were required to traverse along the routes induced unexpected mechanical problems. This was a primary factor in the inability to continuously operate the necessary operating fleet for the planned service on multiple routes. The impacts of terrain on battery charge depletion for BEV deployments will be further addressed in a subsequent edition in this report series. • Sensitivity to physical environment. The impact of the vehicle control system sensitivity to the physical environment also proved a major challenge. During the fall 2021 change of seasons, leaves blowing along the roadways occasionally triggered emergency braking of the shuttles as the sensors identified the leaves as obstacles. • Compliance with ADA regulations. During the deployment, there was an unexpected requirement to strictly comply with Federal Transit Administration ADA regulations. Even though no Federal Transit Administration funds were used, the federal agency required vehicle compliance with its ADA regulations because of the placement of the Denver RTD logo on the vehicles (RTD receives federal funding through the Federal Transit Administration). Major unanticipated expenses were incurred by AV shuttle supplier EasyMile because of the vehicle crash and the other challenges identified previously. There was an associated reduction in the number of vehicles available for the operating fleet, and passenger service levels suffered with only three or four shuttles able to be sustained in operating service (compared to the planned seven-vehicle fleet). The parties involved mutually agreed to terminate the Mines Rover demonstration pilot at the end of the fall 2021 semester rather than continuing to operate the AV routes until the original end-of-pilot date of July 2022.
